resource_envelope.verdict: MEASURED on the rebuild - corroborates the ticket, does not refute it. The ticket recorded a MEASURED 1.22 GiB peak on the real cluster for the batched form (vs 1.23 GiB for the HitPlateStatsBatchQuery sibling) and judged the envelope known-acceptable. Those figures came from the DEV-2409 reference implementation; this ticket is a fresh rebuild, so the open question was whether the rebuilt query keeps that property. It does: on a production-SHAPED local synthetic the leaderboard peaks at 119.33 MiB against the sibling's 295.87 MiB - no worse, in fact lower. The synthetic is ~an order of magnitude smaller than production on read volume, so its absolute MiB values are NOT comparable to the 1.22 GiB cluster figure and do not supersede it; what transfers is the ordering and the mechanism.

production_shaped_synthetic.dataset: 1,950,000 rows, 13 months x 300 kits, 3830 (month,kit) groups, 400,000 distinct plates, scratch database dropped after measurement

resource_envelope.finding: Adding kit_id to the grouping DOES multiply the group count (13 x K instead of 13) and LIMIT 10 BY month genuinely cannot bound it, because it runs post-aggregation. But it does not multiply total aggregate state: the plate population is PARTITIONED across those groups rather than replicated. Measured directly - total uniqExact hash entries identical between the two shapes, with 0 instances of the only replicating mechanism (one plate on multiple kits within a month). Incremental cost is per-group fixed overhead x group count. The trade-off that does appear is CPU time, ~2.4x.
resource_envelope.residual_unknown: Not measured against real production data or real plate/kit skew. Local ClickHouse Cloud access is deliberately never wired into a worktree. The synthetic uses a uniform distribution; a single kit holding an unusually large distinct-plate set would hold a correspondingly larger hash set, though still bounded by that kit's own plate count. Production reference for the sibling shape at the largest org, single month: 1,514,212 read_rows / 83.9 MiB read / 436.4 MiB peak / 69 ms.
resource_envelope.recommendation: The memory concern that drove this AC is resolved. The real trade-off is CPU time (2.4x), which is still a clear win against the 13-call alternative it replaces.

deviations.edit: Phase 3 plan authored by the driver in-session at Opus instead of a dedicated arbiter sub-agent: 3 consecutive HTTP 529 Overloaded on dispatch. Same model tier; deviation recorded rather than downgrading to Sonnet.

Ran the 4 DAG nodes SEQUENTIALLY in REPO_PATH against the single standing isolated env, instead of the flow's per-node git worktree fan-out. Reason: the local ClickHouse databases are the LITERAL shared names clarity/zod (required, because tests/Concerns/RequiresClickhouse TRUNCATEs hardcoded clarity.*/zod.* literals), so two concurrent CH-backed nodes would truncate each other's fixtures and produce false failures. Per-node worktrees would NOT fix this — they would still share the same CH databases — while each additionally costing a full bootstrap (dev:migrate is migrate:fresh + reseed). The DAG is also near-linear (t1||t2 -> t3 -> t4), so serializing costs little. The post-merge full suite + blast-radius re-check still run as specified.

During the fix cycle the driver introduced and then caught a real bug: 'cleaning up' an unused $col by changing `foreach (self::SHARED_PREFIX_MAP as $prefix => $col)` to `as $prefix` silently switched the loop variable from the array KEY to the VALUE, so the cache guard checked keys like 'live_hit_count:unique:...' (always null). Every month was therefore reported uncached, triggering a real fetch that overwrote the seeded sentinels. Three existing tests failed immediately and the cause was diagnosed rather than worked around; fixed with \array_keys(). Recorded because it is exactly the class of silent-semantics change the test suite exists to catch, and because the 'cleanup' was the driver's own, not a worker's.

findings_fixed.finding: StagingLiveHitLeader wrote hardcoded now()->addMinutes(15)/addYear() TTLs into SharedHitStatsData's OWN cross-card keys, bypassing DashboardWidget::getCacheTTL()'s admin_impersonator arm (which collapses BOTH arms to 10 seconds) and using 15 min where the owner uses 10. Because this card renders at array index 2 and the hit cards at 4-7, its write always won: an impersonating staffer would have frozen all four shipped hit cards for a YEAR — during the session opened to verify them — and every org's current-month freshness degraded 10 -> 15 min. Contradicts okf/concepts/impersonation.md and AC-6.
findings_fixed.fix: Added private dashboardCacheTTL(int $index), a verbatim mirror of DashboardWidget::getCacheTTL() including the impersonation arm, and used it for BOTH the card's own buckets and the shared keys. findings_fixed.finding: The shared-key fill loop ran $i >= 0, writing the this_month bucket from HitPlateStatsBatchQuery::handle()'s toStartOfMonth (whole-calendar-month) bucket, whereas SharedHitStatsData::resolveCurrentUniqueMonth() bounds the current month at now(tz)->endOfDay() via handleRange(). The windows differ by up to one UTC offset of the most recent hits, so StagingLiveHits' published 'This Month' number changed for every negative-offset org — and differed between entitled and non-entitled orgs, since a locked card computes nothing. AC-6.
